The ruin of an unfinished Umayyad winter palace about 30 km south of Amman in Jordan, near today's airport. It was probably begun for the caliph al-Walid II during his short reign (743 to 744); a brick found in 1964 bears the name of a man known to have lived between 730 and 750. It is one of the grandest of the Umayyad "desert castles", with Qusayr 'Amra and others, built for control of the land, for hunting and for pleasure.

The palace is a square enclosure with 25 towers in its outer wall. Inside it was divided into three strips, of which only the middle one was built: a gate block with a small mosque, a great courtyard with a pool, and at the far end a hall with three aisles leading to a throne room with three apses under a brick dome, flanked by four suites of vaulted rooms. The middle third of the south front, on either side of the gate, was carved with a deep stone frieze of plants and animals, mixing Classical forms with Sasanian ones: an early example of the blend that became Islamic art.

Work stopped, probably for good when the Abbasids took power in 750 and moved the capital from Damascus to Baghdad. In the early 1900s the Ottoman sultan Abdul Hamid II gave the carved facade to the German emperor Wilhelm II; it was shipped to Berlin, became the start of the city's Museum of Islamic Art in 1904, and now stands in the Pergamon Museum. A bomb in the Second World War destroyed one of its gate towers. The rest of the palace, with part of the east facade, is still on site.
